lessons.title: Context: WWI & the Western Front
lessons.description: Trench warfare, the officer class, shell shock, and Sherriff’s own experience of WWI.
lessons.content_html:
The War Behind the Play

R.C. Sherriff’s Journey’s End (1928) is one of the most important plays ever written about the First World War. Unlike the patriotic propaganda that dominated British culture during 1914–1918, Sherriff’s play presents the war honestly — showing the fear, boredom, exhaustion, and psychological damage that officers endured in the trenches. Sherriff himself served as an officer in the 9th East Surrey Regiment and was wounded at Passchendaele in 1917. The play draws directly on his own experience.

For the Edexcel exam, understanding this context is essential. AO3 requires you to show how the play’s meaning is shaped by the historical period in which it was written and set. Every character, every silence, and every moment of dark humour in the dugout is rooted in the reality of the Western Front.

Key Fact

Sherriff served as a captain in the trenches and was seriously wounded at Passchendaele in 1917. The play is set in a dugout near Saint-Quentin in March 1918, just before the real German Spring Offensive that nearly broke the Allied lines.

Trench Warfare on the Western Front

By 1915 the Western Front had become a continuous line of trenches stretching from the English Channel to Switzerland. Soldiers lived in cramped, muddy, rat-infested conditions. The front-line trenches were supported by communication trenches, reserve trenches, and supply lines. Men rotated between front-line duty, support duty, and brief rest periods behind the lines.

The play captures the monotony and tension of trench life. The characters spend most of their time waiting — eating, talking, sleeping — punctuated by sudden violence when a raid or bombardment begins. This rhythm of boredom and terror is central to the play’s naturalism. Sherriff does not glamorise war; he shows what it actually felt like to sit in a dugout knowing an attack was coming.

The war began in August 1914 and was expected to end quickly. Instead, both sides dug in, and the Western Front barely moved for four years. Key battles include the Somme (1916), where 20,000 British soldiers died on the first day, and Passchendaele (1917), where Sherriff was wounded. By March 1918 — when the play is set — the German army launched its Spring Offensive (Operation Michael), hoping to win before American reinforcements arrived. The play’s final bombardment mirrors this real attack.

The average life expectancy of a junior officer on the front line was just six weeks. Officers were expected to lead from the front, set an example of calm courage, and never show fear to their men. This pressure is exactly what destroys Stanhope in the play.

The Officer Class

All the main characters in Journey’s End are officers — men from the middle and upper classes who were educated at public schools. Stanhope and Raleigh both attended the same school; Osborne was a schoolmaster. The British Army’s officer corps was drawn almost entirely from this social class. They were trained to lead by example, suppress emotion, and maintain a stiff upper lip.

Sherriff shows how these ideals of honour and duty both sustained and crushed the men. Stanhope’s sense of duty keeps him at the front even as alcohol becomes his only coping mechanism. Osborne’s quiet decency makes his death in the raid all the more devastating. The play asks whether the values these men were raised with are adequate for the horrors they face.

Key Fact

The officer class was expected to show courage, self-control, and leadership. Sherriff explores how these ideals both hold the men together and mask the psychological damage beneath the surface. Stanhope’s alcoholism is tolerated because he still does his duty.

Shell Shock and Psychological Damage

Shell shock was one of the most controversial issues of the war. Thousands of soldiers developed symptoms including nightmares, trembling, inability to speak or move, and emotional breakdown. The military establishment was slow to recognise it as a genuine condition — many sufferers were accused of cowardice.

Sherriff never uses the term “shell shock” in the play, but its effects are everywhere. Stanhope drinks to forget. Hibbert invents physical ailments to escape. Even the steady Osborne reveals quiet anxiety. The play shows that psychological damage was not a sign of weakness but an inevitable consequence of prolonged exposure to combat. When Stanhope says, “It’s the only way to forget,” he is describing a coping mechanism shared by thousands of real officers.

When Journey’s End premiered in December 1928, a decade after the Armistice, audiences were ready to confront the reality of the war. The play was an immediate sensation — transferring to the West End in January 1929 and running for nearly 600 performances. Critics praised its honesty and restraint. Unlike earlier war literature that either glorified combat or descended into bitterness, Sherriff presented ordinary men doing their best in impossible circumstances.

The play appeared alongside other landmark works of war literature: Erich Maria Remarque’s All Quiet on the Western Front (1929), Siegfried Sassoon’s Memoirs of an Infantry Officer (1930), and Wilfred Owen’s posthumous poetry. Together, these works created a cultural shift in how Britain remembered the war — moving from patriotic pride to a more honest reckoning with its human cost.

Sherriff’s Dramatic Approach

Sherriff chose to set his entire play inside a single dugout over a period of just four days (Monday to Thursday). There are no battle scenes on stage, no grand speeches, and no villains. The war is experienced through the men’s conversations, their silences, and the sounds of shelling from above. This stripped-back approach forces the audience to focus on the human cost of war rather than its spectacle. The setting itself becomes a kind of trap — the men cannot leave, and the audience shares their confinement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the Edexcel exam, Section B gives you a short quotation from Journey’s End and asks you to write an essay about a character or theme. AO3 (context) is worth up to 20 of the 40 content marks, so you must weave historical context into every paragraph — not bolt it on at the end. Instead of writing “soldiers suffered in WWI,” connect context to specific moments: “Stanhope’s alcoholism reflects the widespread reliance on alcohol among officers who had no other way to cope with prolonged front-line duty.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sherriff served in the trenches and was wounded at Passchendaele — the play draws directly on his own experience of the Western Front.
  • The officer class was expected to suppress fear and show courage; the play explores how these ideals both sustain and damage the characters.
  • Shell shock (now PTSD) is central to the play, even though the term is never used — Stanhope’s drinking, Hibbert’s feigned illness, and Osborne’s quiet anxiety all reflect its effects.

lessons.title: Act 1: Arrival in the Trenches
lessons.description: Raleigh’s arrival, Stanhope’s alcoholism, Osborne as the ‘uncle’, and the dugout setting.
lessons.content_html:
The Opening of the Play

Act 1 of Journey’s End establishes everything the audience needs to know: the setting, the characters, and the central tensions that will drive the drama. The curtain rises on a dugout in the British trenches near Saint-Quentin, March 1918. Captain Hardy is handing over the position to Osborne, and through their conversation we learn about the company, its commander Stanhope, and the German attack that everyone knows is coming.

Sherriff uses this handover scene as a form of exposition. Rather than telling the audience directly what has happened, he lets the characters reveal it through natural conversation. Hardy’s casual gossip about Stanhope’s drinking, Osborne’s loyal defence of his captain, and the details about trench routines all feel like real speech — not staged information. This naturalistic approach is one of the play’s greatest strengths.

Key Fact

Before Stanhope appears on stage, Hardy tells Osborne that he drinks constantly: “I never did see a youngster put away the whisky he does.” This prepares the audience to judge Stanhope harshly — but Osborne immediately defends him, creating a tension between reputation and reality that runs through the entire play.

Stanhope — The Damaged Leader

Stanhope is the company commander, just twenty-one years old, and he has been at the front for three years without a break. He is the longest-serving officer in the battalion. His alcoholism is an open secret — Hardy jokes about it, and Osborne acknowledges it — but his men respect him because he still performs his duties with fierce dedication.

When Stanhope finally appears, he is tense, irritable, and immediately reaches for the whisky. His key Act 1 line captures the desperate necessity of the habit: “She doesn’t know that if I went up those steps into the front line — without being doped with whiskey — I’d go mad with fright.” This tells us that Stanhope is self-aware — he knows he is damaged — but sees alcohol as his only means of functioning. The whisky is not a luxury; it is survival. Sherriff shows that the war has pushed this young man beyond his limits, and the prospect of facing the front line sober is, for Stanhope, unthinkable.

Stanhope’s reaction to Raleigh’s arrival is not pleasure but anxiety. He is terrified that Raleigh will write home and tell his sister — Stanhope’s fiancée, Madge — about his drinking and deterioration. He confides his fear to Osborne, revealing how precarious his grip on composure has become. He has maintained a facade of competence for three years, and Raleigh’s innocent admiration threatens to expose the truth. Note: Stanhope’s explosive outburst “To forget, you little fool — to forget! … You think there’s no limit to what a man can bear?” belongs to Act 3 Scene 2, after Osborne’s death — not Act 1.

Stanhope’s plan to censor Raleigh’s letters shows how desperate he is to control his image. It also creates dramatic irony: the audience knows that Raleigh’s letter, when it finally comes, will be full of admiration, not criticism. Stanhope’s fear is unfounded — but the fact that he cannot see this tells us how profoundly the war has distorted his thinking.

Raleigh — The Innocent Newcomer

Second Lieutenant Raleigh is fresh from England, young, enthusiastic, and eager to serve under Stanhope, whom he hero-worships from school. He used his connections (“uncle” in the military) to get posted to Stanhope’s company. Raleigh represents the naïve idealism that many young men brought to the war — and that the trenches would destroy.

Raleigh’s line “How awfully nice — if the Dosch didn’t tell — and Dosch didn’t know” reveals his boyish excitement at being posted near Stanhope. He treats the war like a school adventure. The gap between Raleigh’s enthusiasm and Stanhope’s exhaustion creates one of the play’s central dramatic tensions. Sherriff uses Raleigh as a mirror: through Raleigh’s eyes, we see what Stanhope once was before the war changed him.

Key Fact

Raleigh hero-worships Stanhope from school: in his letter home, he calls him “the finest officer in the battalion — the men simply love him.” Meanwhile, Stanhope’s closest confidant is Osborne — it is Stanhope who, in Act 3 Scene 2 (after Osborne’s death), cries out “the one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man — who understood everything.” These are two separate quotes by different characters in different acts. Stanhope sees Raleigh as a threat who might expose his deterioration — a contrast between past innocence and present damage that drives the play’s emotional core.

Osborne — “Uncle”

Lieutenant Osborne is the oldest officer in the company, a former schoolmaster, and universally known as “uncle.” He is calm, kind, and steady — the emotional anchor of the group. While Stanhope leads through fierce willpower and Raleigh through naïve enthusiasm, Osborne leads through quiet decency. He reads Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland before the raid, a detail that humanises him and makes his death all the more devastating.

Osborne’s role in Act 1 is crucial. He defends Stanhope to Hardy, reassures Raleigh, and gently manages the tension between them. He is Stanhope’s confidant — the only person Stanhope trusts. Osborne tells Raleigh about the earwig races and makes the dugout feel almost homely, yet beneath his calm exterior, there are hints of strain. Sherriff uses Osborne to show that even the most composed men are carrying unbearable weight.

The entire play takes place in a single dugout. Sherriff’s stage directions describe a cramped space with earth walls, a table, and candlelight. The dugout functions as a microcosm of the war: the officers are trapped, unable to leave, forced to wait for an attack they know is coming. The confined space intensifies every relationship and every conflict.

The sounds of war — distant shelling, rifle fire, the rumble of artillery — are heard offstage but never seen. This technique keeps the violence just out of sight, making it more menacing. The audience, like the characters, can only listen and wait. Sherriff’s decision to keep all action within the dugout was radical for 1928 and reflects the real experience of officers, who spent far more time waiting than fighting.

Dramatic Techniques in Act 1

Act 1 establishes the play’s distinctive dramatic style. The dialogue is natural and understated — characters talk about food, earwig races, and bed arrangements rather than grand themes. Yet beneath this ordinary conversation, Sherriff layers fear, tension, and psychological complexity. The technique of understatement is central to the play. When Hardy describes the previous company’s losses with a casual “Cheero,” the gap between his cheerful tone and the horror he describes creates a powerful emotional effect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam gives you a quotation from Act 1, use it as a springboard to discuss character relationships and dramatic technique. For example, if the quotation is about Stanhope’s drinking, analyse the language closely (AO1), then connect it to the wider theme of psychological damage (AO3). Always zoom out from the quotation to the play as a whole — the best essays move between close analysis and broader argument.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Act 1 uses the Hardy–Osborne handover as exposition, revealing Stanhope’s alcoholism, the approaching attack, and the dynamics of the company through natural dialogue.
  • Stanhope, Raleigh, and Osborne represent three responses to war: damaged endurance, naïve idealism, and quiet resilience.
  • The dugout setting creates confinement, and Sherriff’s use of understatement, offstage sound, and naturalistic dialogue builds tension beneath the surface.

lessons.title: Act 2: Tensions & the Raid
lessons.description: The raid preparations, Stanhope’s letter censorship, Hibbert’s cowardice, and rising tension.
lessons.content_html:
Act 2 — The Pressure Builds

Act 2 of Journey’s End deepens the tensions established in Act 1. The German attack is now imminent, and the Colonel arrives with orders for a dangerous trench raid. Stanhope must send men across no man’s land to capture a German prisoner for intelligence. This act also contains two of the play’s most important scenes: Stanhope’s decision to censor Raleigh’s letter, and Hibbert’s attempt to leave the front line by claiming illness.

Sherriff structures Act 2 around the theme of duty versus self-preservation. Every character is forced to choose between obeying orders and protecting themselves or the people they care about. The raid hangs over the act like a sentence of death, and the audience watches the men respond in different ways: Osborne with quiet acceptance, Stanhope with fierce control, Hibbert with desperate evasion, and Raleigh with naïve willingness.

Key Fact

The Colonel orders the raid to capture a German soldier for intelligence about the expected attack. Stanhope objects to sending Osborne on such a dangerous mission, but the Colonel insists. This reveals the military hierarchy’s disregard for individual lives — decisions made from behind the lines directly cause the deaths of men the audience has come to care about.

The Censorship Scene

One of Act 2’s most revealing scenes occurs when Stanhope insists on reading Raleigh’s letter home before it is sent. He has been dreading this moment — convinced that Raleigh will describe his censorship of his own letters was a real practice during WWI, and Sherriff uses it here to create dramatic irony.

When Osborne reads the letter aloud, it contains nothing but admiration: Raleigh describes Stanhope as “the best company commander in the battalion” and says how proud he is to serve under him. Stanhope is stunned and ashamed. The moment is devastating because it reveals the gap between Stanhope’s tortured self-image and how others actually see him. He has been so consumed by guilt and fear that he cannot recognise loyalty when it is offered.

Stanhope’s insistence on censoring the letter exposes his deepest fear: not the Germans, not death, but being seen as he truly is. His identity is split between the heroic schoolboy Raleigh remembers and the alcoholic wreck he believes himself to be. The dramatic irony is powerful — the audience already suspects that Raleigh’s letter will be positive, but Stanhope cannot imagine it. His shame has so distorted his perception that he is incapable of trusting anyone’s good opinion of him.

After hearing the letter, Stanhope quietly says he will not censor it after all. This small moment of grace is one of the few times in the play where Stanhope lets his guard down. Sherriff shows that beneath the toughness, Stanhope is still capable of being moved — but the war has made vulnerability feel like a threat.

Hibbert’s Attempt to Leave

Second Lieutenant Hibbert claims he has neuralgia (severe headaches) and asks to be sent to the rear. Stanhope sees through the excuse immediately and confronts Hibbert in one of the play’s most intense scenes. He tells Hibbert that every officer is afraid — including himself — and threatens to shoot him if he tries to leave.

This scene is crucial because it shows Stanhope at his most complex. He is simultaneously cruel (threatening to shoot a fellow officer) and honest (admitting his own fear). When he says that he, too, has considered pretending to be ill, he strips away the mask of the fearless leader. The scene also raises an uncomfortable moral question: is Hibbert a coward, or simply a man who has reached his breaking point? Sherriff refuses to give a simple answer. Hibbert’s fear is real, even if his excuse is not.

Key Fact

Stanhope tells Hibbert: “If you went — and left Osborne and Trotter and Raleigh and all the other men who are staying here — I’d rather spare you than any of them.” threatens to shoot Hibbert if he leaves, but then admits his own terror. The scene ends with both men agreeing to go on together. Sherriff shows that courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to carry on despite it.

The Raid Preparations

The Colonel selects Osborne and Raleigh to lead the raiding party. Stanhope objects, not wanting to risk Osborne, but the Colonel dismisses his concerns. This moment reveals the callousness of military command: the Colonel is more interested in capturing a prisoner than in the lives of the men he sends. He offers Osborne a box of cigars as a reward, a detail that highlights the grotesque disparity between the commanders behind the lines and the men who face death.

The night before the raid, Osborne and Raleigh sit together in the dugout. Osborne reads aloud from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, and they talk about England, home, and mundane things. This quiet domestic scene, set against the knowledge that one or both may die tomorrow, is one of Sherriff’s most effective dramatic techniques. The contrast between the ordinariness of their conversation and the horror of what awaits them creates unbearable tension.

Osborne’s choice of reading material is significant. Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland is a children’s book about a nonsensical world where normal rules do not apply. There is a clear parallel with the war: the officers have fallen into their own nightmarish wonderland where death is random and authority makes no sense. The book also connects to Osborne’s former life as a schoolmaster — it is a reminder of the civilised, orderly world he has left behind.

By having Osborne read a children’s book just before he goes to his death, Sherriff emphasises his innocence and gentleness. It also functions as a form of escape: Osborne retreats into a fantasy world rather than facing the reality of the next day. The scene is profoundly moving because it shows a good man quietly preparing to die.

Themes in Act 2

Act 2 brings several key themes into sharp focus. The conflict between duty and self-preservation is dramatised through Hibbert. The gap between the military command and the men on the ground is shown through the Colonel’s casual ordering of the raid. The theme of appearance versus reality deepens as Stanhope’s fear is contrasted with his outward authority, and Raleigh’s admiring letter reveals the disconnect between Stanhope’s self-image and how he is perceived. Every scene in Act 2 tightens the pressure towards the inevitable catastrophe of the raid.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Act 2 is rich material for the Section B essay. If asked about a theme like courage or fear, use the Stanhope–Hibbert scene — it offers quotations, character analysis, and clear AO3 links (shell shock, cowardice in WWI, the threat of execution). Always analyse specific language choices: why does Stanhope say “if you went” rather than “if you leave”? The conditional tense carries menace while maintaining the understatement typical of officer-class speech.

Key Takeaways

  • The censorship scene creates dramatic irony: Stanhope expects criticism in Raleigh’s letter but finds only admiration, revealing how guilt and shame have distorted his self-perception.
  • The Stanhope–Hibbert confrontation explores the fine line between courage and cowardice — Stanhope threatens to shoot Hibbert, then admits his own fear.
  • Osborne reading Alice in Wonderland before the raid creates a poignant contrast between innocence and impending death, and symbolises the absurdity of war.

lessons.title: Act 3: The Raid, Death & the Ending
lessons.description: Osborne’s death, the bitter dinner scene, Raleigh’s death, and the final bombardment.
lessons.content_html:
Act 3 — Loss and Destruction

Act 3 of Journey’s End contains the play’s most devastating moments. The raid takes place offstage, and Osborne is killed. The surviving officers are expected to carry on as if nothing has happened, and the Colonel sends champagne and cigars to celebrate the capture of a German prisoner. Meanwhile, Raleigh is bewildered and heartbroken by the callous response to Osborne’s death. By the end of the act, the German bombardment begins, Raleigh is fatally wounded, and the dugout is destroyed. Sherriff’s restraint makes these scenes more powerful — there are no heroic speeches, only the quiet horror of men being destroyed by a war they cannot escape.

Key Fact

Osborne’s death occurs offstage during the raid. The audience never sees it. Sherriff’s decision to keep the violence unseen is a deliberate dramatic choice: it mirrors how the officers in the dugout experience the war (hearing it, not seeing it) and makes the loss more devastating because the audience must process it through the survivors’ reactions.

The Raid and Osborne’s Death

Osborne and Raleigh lead the raid. Only Raleigh and a German prisoner return. Osborne is dead. The audience has spent the entire play getting to know this kind, steady man — his Alice in Wonderland, his earwig races, his quiet defence of Stanhope — and now he is gone. Sherriff does not describe how Osborne died. There is no grand final speech. Raleigh simply returns, stunned and barely able to speak, and the other officers piece together what happened from fragments of information.

This is one of Sherriff’s most powerful techniques: the absence of detail. By refusing to show Osborne’s death, Sherriff forces the audience to imagine it. The effect is more disturbing than any battlefield scene could be. It also reflects the real experience of war: officers in the dugout often learned of deaths through brief, incomplete reports rather than witnessing them directly.

The Celebration Dinner

After the raid, the Colonel sends champagne, cigars, and congratulations. The surviving officers sit down to dinner. This is one of the most bitter and ironic scenes in the play. Stanhope, Trotter, and Hibbert eat and drink while Osborne’s empty chair sits at the table. Stanhope forces himself to be cheerful, almost manic, drinking heavily and making jokes. The celebration feels grotesque — a man has just died, and they are expected to toast the mission’s success.

Raleigh refuses to join the dinner. He is appalled that the others can eat and drink after Osborne’s death. Stanhope rounds on him furiously: the implication is that Stanhope is not celebrating — he is trying to survive. The whisky and forced cheerfulness are coping mechanisms, not callousness. Raleigh’s refusal, while morally understandable, shows his naïveté: he does not yet understand that in the trenches, you must eat, drink, and carry on, because tomorrow you may be dead too.

This confrontation is the climax of the Stanhope–Raleigh relationship. Raleigh says he cannot eat when Osborne is dead. Stanhope explodes, telling Raleigh that he is not the only one who cared about Osborne — that Stanhope is suffering too, but has to keep going. The scene reveals that Stanhope’s apparent hardness is a survival strategy. His fury comes from grief, not indifference.

Sherriff uses this scene to challenge the audience’s assumptions. If we sympathise with Raleigh’s moral outrage, we must also understand that Stanhope’s response is the only way a front-line officer can function. Neither man is wrong. The tragedy is that the war has made normal human responses — grief, outrage, compassion — impossible to sustain.

Raleigh’s Death

In the play’s final scene, the German bombardment begins. Raleigh is brought into the dugout with a spinal wound. He cannot feel his legs. Stanhope, who has been angry with Raleigh since the dinner scene, now becomes tender and gentle. He lies Raleigh on Osborne’s bed — a detail loaded with symbolic weight — and sits beside him. Raleigh whispers that it is getting dark, and Stanhope quietly says “It’s just the light — it’s nearly morning.”

Raleigh dies. Stanhope is called up to the front. A shell hits the dugout, and the stage directions describe the roof caving in, the candle going out, and “the whine of a shell rising to a shriek.” The play ends not with a speech or a resolution, but with devastation. Sherriff offers no comfort, no meaning, no redemption. The war simply destroys everything.

Key Fact

Raleigh dies on Osborne’s bed, symbolising the cycle of death that the war endlessly repeats. Stanhope’s tenderness in this final scene — after his earlier anger — shows that he has never stopped caring. The play ends with the dugout’s destruction, offering no resolution or redemption.

The Ending — No Resolution

The final moments of the play are striking for what they do not contain. There is no final speech. No character reflects on the meaning of their sacrifice. The stage simply goes dark as the bombardment overwhelms the dugout. Sherriff’s refusal to provide catharsis is a deliberate artistic choice. The war does not offer tidy endings, and neither does the play. The audience is left with the same feelings as the characters: loss, helplessness, and the absence of meaning.

When Raleigh is dying, Stanhope’s entire manner changes. The anger, the sarcasm, the defensive toughness all fall away, and we see the real Stanhope: a young man capable of great gentleness. He places Raleigh on Osborne’s bed, holds his hand, and speaks softly. His lie — “It’s just the light — it’s nearly morning” — is both a comfort and a final act of protection. The darkness Raleigh feels is death approaching, but Stanhope cannot say that.

This scene reconciles the two men and reveals the depth of Stanhope’s suppressed emotion. Everything he has kept locked away — grief for Osborne, guilt, love for Raleigh as a friend — surfaces in these final moments. Sherriff shows that the war has not destroyed Stanhope’s humanity; it has merely buried it under layers of self-protection.

The play’s final image — the collapsing dugout, the extinguished candle, the rising shriek of shells — is a powerful visual metaphor for the destruction of an entire generation. Sherriff closes the play not with words but with sounds and darkness, leaving the audience to confront the war’s waste on their own terms.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Act 3 offers the strongest material for Section B essays on themes like loss, futility, or friendship. The celebration dinner is especially useful: it allows you to discuss dramatic irony, characterisation, and AO3 context (how officers coped) all in one paragraph. Practise writing about what is not said or shown — Sherriff’s use of silence, offstage action, and absence is as important as his dialogue.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Osborne’s death is kept offstage, forcing the audience to experience the loss through the survivors’ reactions rather than through spectacle.
  • The celebration dinner is bitterly ironic — Stanhope drinks and jokes to survive, while Raleigh’s refusal to eat shows he has not yet learned the rules of trench endurance.
  • Raleigh dies on Osborne’s bed, Stanhope shows tenderness for the first time, and the play ends without resolution — the dugout is destroyed, offering no comfort or meaning.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Stanhope, Osborne, Raleigh, Trotter, Hibbert, Mason, and the Colonel analysed in depth.
lessons.content_html:
Characters in Journey’s End

Sherriff populates his dugout with a carefully chosen group of characters who represent different responses to war. For the Edexcel exam, you need to be able to write about how each character is presented, what they reveal about the play’s themes, and how Sherriff uses them to explore the effects of conflict on individuals. Remember that Section B tests AO1 (your response and use of quotations) and AO3 (context), so always link character analysis to the historical period.

Captain Stanhope

Stanhope is the protagonist and the most complex character in the play. He is twenty-one years old, has been at the front for three years without leave, and is the longest-serving officer in the battalion. He is a brilliant and dedicated commander — the Colonel calls him “the best company commander in the battalion” — but he is also an alcoholic who drinks to suppress the psychological damage of prolonged combat.

Stanhope’s central conflict is between the person he was (a popular, heroic schoolboy) and the person the war has made him (a traumatised, dependent wreck). His fear about Raleigh’s letter reveals this split: he is terrified that his fiancée Madge will learn the truth. His line “You think there’s no limit to what a man can bear?” is the play’s most direct expression of psychological breaking point.

Key Fact

Stanhope’s alcoholism is not weakness but survival. He says: “It’s the only way to forget.” Sherriff presents a young man who has been pushed beyond his limits by a war that offers no support for mental health. His fierce loyalty, his tenderness with the dying Raleigh, and his refusal to leave the front all show that duty and damage can coexist.

Osborne is the oldest officer in the company, a former schoolmaster and rugby player, and the emotional heart of the group. He is nicknamed “uncle” because of his paternal, caring nature. He defends Stanhope to Hardy, reassures Raleigh, reads Alice in Wonderland, and organises earwig races — small acts of kindness that hold the group together.

Osborne represents the gentlemanly ideal: calm, decent, selfless. His death during the raid is the play’s emotional turning point. Sherriff kills the most universally loved character to show that war does not spare the good. Osborne’s reading of Alice in Wonderland before the raid connects his innocence to the absurdity of the world he is about to enter — a world where decency offers no protection.

Second Lieutenant Raleigh

Raleigh is the youngest and most inexperienced officer, fresh from England and eager to serve. He hero-worships Stanhope from their school days and pulled strings to be posted to his company. Raleigh functions as the audience’s entry point into the world of the trenches: his naïveté mirrors our own unfamiliarity, and his gradual loss of innocence mirrors the broader disillusionment caused by the war.

Raleigh admires Stanhope deeply, though it is Stanhope who later describes Osborne as “the one man I could trust — my best friend”” establishes the schoolboy bond that Stanhope fears the war has destroyed. His refusal to eat at the dinner after Osborne’s death shows genuine moral feeling, but also reveals his inability to understand the coping mechanisms that front-line soldiers need. His death on Osborne’s bed completes his journey from innocent to casualty, and Stanhope’s tenderness in that scene finally reconciles the two men.

Trotter is a cheerful, uncomplicated officer from a lower-middle-class background. He talks constantly about food, draws circles on a chart to count down the hours of each duty period, and provides comic relief through his blunt, good-natured personality. His coping mechanism is to focus on small, tangible pleasures — the next meal, the next rest period — rather than thinking about the bigger picture.

Trotter is often underestimated in exam answers, but he is important. He represents the ordinary soldier who survives by not thinking too deeply. His promotion to replace Osborne after the raid shows that the war values endurance over sensitivity. Sherriff uses Trotter to contrast with the more emotionally complex Stanhope and Osborne — his simplicity is both his strength and his limitation.

Second Lieutenant Hibbert

Hibbert is the most controversial character in the play. He claims to have neuralgia and asks to be sent to the rear, but Stanhope sees through his excuse and threatens to shoot him. Hibbert represents the fear that every soldier felt but most suppressed. His attempt to escape is not simply cowardice; it is a human response to intolerable conditions.

What makes Hibbert interesting is that Stanhope admits he has felt the same way. The difference between them is not that Stanhope is braver — it is that Stanhope’s sense of duty is stronger. Sherriff blurs the line between courage and cowardice, suggesting that both are responses to the same impossible situation. Hibbert challenges the audience to consider whether they would behave any differently.

Key Fact

Hibbert and Stanhope are two sides of the same coin. Both are terrified. Stanhope stays because of duty and alcohol; Hibbert tries to leave because he has no coping mechanism. Sherriff asks whether the line between courage and cowardice is really as clear as the military system demands.

Mason is the officers’ cook and batman. He provides gentle comic relief through his complaints about the quality of food (“a yellow sort of stuff, sir”) and his earnest attempts to make the best of terrible supplies. Mason humanises the dugout and reminds the audience that even in war, people cling to the routines of normal life.

The Colonel represents the military hierarchy. He orders the dangerous raid, dismisses Stanhope’s objections about sending Osborne, and sends champagne to celebrate the capture of a prisoner — apparently indifferent to Osborne’s death. The Colonel is not a villain, but his detachment from the human cost of his orders illustrates the gap between those who give commands and those who carry them out.

Together, these characters form a cross-section of the officer class: the heroic wreck (Stanhope), the steady mentor (Osborne), the innocent newcomer (Raleigh), the cheerful pragmatist (Trotter), the man at breaking point (Hibbert), and the detached authority (the Colonel). Each responds to the war differently, and Sherriff uses their contrasts to explore the full range of human responses to conflict.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Character questions in Section B often ask you to explore how a character is presented — this means discussing Sherriff’s choices as a playwright, not just what the character does. Always include: what the character says (close quotation analysis), what others say about them, their dramatic function (e.g. Raleigh as audience surrogate), and how they connect to AO3 context (the officer class, shell shock, the military hierarchy).

  • Sherriff blurs the line between courage and cowardice — the Stanhope–Hibbert confrontation shows that both men are afraid, and the only difference is their coping mechanism.

lessons.title: Setting, Staging & Dramatic Techniques
lessons.description: The dugout as microcosm, real-time structure, offstage action, sound effects, and naturalism.
lessons.content_html:
Setting, Staging, and Dramatic Techniques

One of the most striking features of Journey’s End is what it does not show. There are no battle scenes, no no man’s land sequences, no dramatic charges. The entire play takes place inside a single underground dugout over four days. Sherriff’s decision to confine his play to this cramped, candlelit space was radical in 1928, and it remains one of the most important aspects of the play for the Edexcel exam. Understanding how Sherriff tells the story is just as important as understanding what happens.

The Dugout as Microcosm

The dugout functions as a microcosm of the entire war. Inside its earth walls, we see the officer class in miniature: the tensions between duty and self-preservation, the hierarchy of command, the coping mechanisms, and the bonds of friendship that sustain the men. Everything that matters about the Western Front experience is compressed into this single room.

The setting also creates a powerful sense of claustrophobia. The men cannot leave. The audience cannot see beyond the earth walls. The war exists as sound — distant shells, rifle fire, the rumble of artillery — but is never visible. Sherriff traps both the characters and the audience in the same confined space, forcing both to experience the war through its indirect effects: waiting, listening, and imagining the worst.

Key Fact

The dugout is not just a backdrop — it is a dramatic device. By confining the entire play to one room, Sherriff mirrors the entrapment of trench warfare. The audience shares the officers’ experience of confinement, boredom, and anxiety, making the play’s impact visceral rather than intellectual.

Real-Time Structure

The play covers four days, from Monday evening to Thursday morning. This near real-time structure creates extraordinary tension. The audience knows from Act 1 that the German attack is expected on Thursday. As each act passes — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday night, Thursday dawn — the deadline approaches, and the pressure becomes almost unbearable.

This structure also means there is no escape. Unlike a play that covers weeks or months, Journey’s End offers no time jumps where the characters might recover or circumstances might change. The relentless forward movement of time mirrors the officers’ own experience: they cannot go back, and the attack is coming whether they are ready or not. The compressed time frame gives the play the quality of a countdown.

Almost all of the play’s violence happens offstage. The raid, Osborne’s death, and the final bombardment are experienced through sound: the crack of rifles, the thud of explosions, the whine of incoming shells. Sherriff’s stage directions are precise about these sounds, specifying their volume, duration, and proximity.

This technique has several effects. First, it keeps the focus on the characters’ reactions rather than on spectacle. Second, it mirrors the real experience of trench officers, who spent most of their time underground, hearing the war rather than seeing it. Third, it makes the violence more frightening, because what the audience cannot see must be imagined. The final stage direction — “the whine of a shell rising to a shriek” followed by the collapse of the dugout — is more powerful for being heard, not shown.

Naturalism and Understatement

Sherriff writes in the naturalistic tradition. His characters speak as real people do — they talk about food, complain about the weather, make jokes, and avoid discussing their deepest fears. There are no soliloquies, no asides to the audience, and no moments where characters articulate their feelings in poetic language. The emotional impact comes from what is not said.

This understatement is central to the play’s power. When Hardy says “Cheero” while describing the previous company’s devastating losses, the gap between his cheerful tone and the horror he describes creates a deeply unsettling effect. When Osborne talks about earwig races hours before a raid that may kill him, the audience feels the weight of what he is not saying. Sherriff trusts the audience to read between the lines.

Key Fact

Hardy’s casual “Cheero” while describing death, Osborne’s earwig races before the raid, and Stanhope’s forced joking at the dinner all use understatement. The gap between what is said and what is felt creates the play’s distinctive emotional power — the audience must infer the characters’ true feelings from their behaviour, not their words.

Stage Directions and Lighting

Sherriff’s stage directions are unusually detailed. He specifies the yellow candlelight, the shadows on the earth walls, the sound of distant guns, and the time of day. The lighting is almost entirely candlelight, which creates a warm but fragile atmosphere — the candle can be extinguished at any moment, just as the characters’ lives can. When the candle goes out in the final scene, it is a visual symbol of the destruction of everything the audience has watched for two hours.

Sherriff uses dramatic irony throughout the play. The 1928 audience knew what happened in March 1918: the German Spring Offensive nearly broke the Allied line, and thousands of men were killed. When the characters discuss the expected attack, the audience already knows its scale and devastation. This foreknowledge intensifies every ordinary moment — every meal, every joke, every conversation about home — because the audience knows it may be the character’s last.

The letter scene also uses dramatic irony: the audience suspects that Raleigh’s letter will praise Stanhope, but Stanhope fears the worst. These layers of knowledge create a tension that the characters themselves cannot feel, drawing the audience deeper into the emotional experience.

Sherriff’s combination of a confined setting, near real-time structure, offstage violence, naturalistic dialogue, and pervasive understatement creates a play that feels less like a performance and more like an experience. The audience does not watch the war — they share it. This is what makes Journey’s End one of the most enduring and powerful works of war literature.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Dramatic technique is tested through AO1, but the best responses connect technique to context (AO3). For example: “Sherriff’s use of offstage violence reflects the real experience of officers who heard the war more than they saw it. By keeping the raid unseen, Sherriff mirrors the limited, fragmented way that news of death actually reached the dugout.” This kind of response embeds context into analysis of form, which is what top-level answers do.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The dugout setting is a microcosm of the war, confining both characters and audience in a claustrophobic space where the violence is heard but never seen.
  • The near real-time structure (four days) creates a countdown to the attack, building relentless tension with no possibility of escape or recovery.
  • Naturalism and understatement are the play’s defining techniques — the gap between what is said and what is felt creates emotional power that is stronger than any dramatic speech could achieve.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Heroism, fear, class, friendship, futility of war, and exam technique for Section B.
lessons.content_html:
Key Themes in Journey’s End

Your modern-text essay will always focus on a character, theme, or relationship. Themes run through the entire play, so your essay must range across all three acts — not just one scene. This lesson brings together the play’s major themes and shows you how to structure them into exam-ready arguments. Each theme is supported by key quotations that you should memorise for the closed-book exam.

Heroism and Duty

Sherriff presents heroism not as a grand quality but as the quiet, exhausting act of carrying on. Stanhope is called the best company commander in the battalion, yet he is an alcoholic who can barely function without whisky. Osborne’s heroism lies in his calm decency and willingness to lead the raid despite knowing the danger. Even Trotter is heroic in his own way — his determination to focus on the next meal rather than on fear is a survival strategy that keeps him and others grounded.

The play redefines heroism: it is not the absence of fear, but the decision to continue despite it. Stanhope tells Hibbert that every officer is afraid. The difference between them is not bravery but duty — Stanhope’s sense of duty keeps him at the front even when every instinct tells him to leave. Sherriff asks whether this version of heroism is admirable or simply a form of entrapment imposed by social expectations.

Key Fact

Sherriff redefines heroism as endurance, not glory. Stanhope’s heroism is inseparable from his damage. He drinks to endure what most cannot face.e play suggests that the real heroism of WWI was not found in dramatic charges but in the daily, grinding act of carrying on when every part of you wants to stop.

Fear and Coping

Every character in the play is afraid, but each copes differently. Stanhope uses alcohol. Osborne uses routine and calm. Trotter uses food and humour. Hibbert tries to escape. Raleigh, at first, does not understand fear because he has not yet experienced the reality of the front. Sherriff uses these contrasting responses to argue that fear is universal — the only question is how you manage it.

The Stanhope–Hibbert confrontation is the play’s most direct exploration of this theme. Stanhope threatens to shoot Hibbert, then admits: “I feel the same — exactly the same.” This moment strips away the idea that courage is a fixed character trait. Instead, Sherriff presents it as a daily choice, made harder by the absence of any support system for psychological damage. The military offered no treatment for what we now call PTSD; the only options were to endure, to drink, or to break.

All the officers in Journey’s End are from the middle or upper-middle class, educated at public schools. Stanhope and Raleigh attended the same school; Osborne was a schoolmaster. The public-school system trained boys for leadership through sport, discipline, and the suppression of emotion. These values — the stiff upper lip, team spirit, duty before self — are both the source of the officers’ strength and the cause of their suffering.

Trotter is the exception: he comes from a lower-middle-class background and is less polished than the others. His promotion to replace Osborne after the raid subtly suggests that the class system is breaking down under the pressure of war — competence matters more than background. The Colonel, meanwhile, represents the upper echelons of the military hierarchy, issuing orders from behind the lines with little regard for the cost to the men who carry them out.

Friendship and Brotherhood

The bonds between the men are the play’s emotional core. Stanhope and Osborne share a deep, unspoken understanding — Osborne is the only person Stanhope trusts. The Stanhope–Raleigh relationship is more complicated: it is built on a school friendship that the war has distorted. Stanhope describes Osborne as “the one man I could trust — my best friend — the one man I could talk to as man to man,”t the Stanhope he finds is a damaged stranger who sees Raleigh as a threat.

Sherriff shows that camaraderie is both the men’s greatest comfort and the source of their greatest pain. Osborne’s death devastates Stanhope precisely because they were close. Stanhope’s tenderness with dying Raleigh shows that the friendship was real all along, but the war made it impossible to express. The play suggests that love and loss in wartime are inseparable.

Futility pervades the play. The raid is carried out at great cost — Osborne dies — to capture a single German prisoner whose information changes nothing. The German attack comes anyway. Raleigh dies. The dugout is destroyed. The play ends without resolution, suggesting that the suffering was meaningless.

Sherriff does not make this argument through speeches or moralising. Instead, he shows it through structure: the play ends where it began, with the sound of shells and the darkness of the dugout. Nothing has been gained. The cycle of duty, fear, loss, and death simply continues. This structural futility mirrors the wider futility of the Western Front, where millions died for gains measured in yards.

Key Fact

The play’s themes work together: heroism is undermined by futility, friendship is destroyed by loss, and the class system that creates leaders also destroys them. The best exam essays explore these connections rather than treating themes in isolation.

Exam Technique — The Modern-Text Essay

A typical modern-text essay question gives you a short quotation from the play and asks you to write an essay. You will often choose one question from two. The question will focus on a character, theme, or relationship. It is a closed-book exam, so you must memorise quotations. Here is a step-by-step approach:

Step 1 — Read the quotation carefully. Identify the character, theme, or idea it relates to. Underline key words in the question.

Step 2 — Plan three to four paragraphs. Each paragraph should make a different point about the question. Aim to cover different parts of the play (not just one act). Each paragraph needs: a point, a quotation (embedded, not bolted on), analysis of language, and a link to context (AO3).

Step 3 — Use the quotation as a springboard. Start your first paragraph by engaging with the given quotation. Analyse its language closely. Then move outwards to other parts of the play.

Step 4 — Embed context into analysis. Do not write a separate “context paragraph.” Instead, weave AO3 into every paragraph: “Stanhope’s reliance on alcohol reflects the widespread use of whisky among officers who had no other support for what we now recognise as PTSD.”

Step 5 — Conclude briefly. Sum up your argument in two to three sentences. Do not introduce new evidence.

The assessment objectives for the modern-text essay typically include: AO1 — your response to the text, supported by quotations and references; AO3 — understanding of context (historical, social, cultural); and AO4 — spelling, punctuation, and grammar alongside accurate use of literary terminology. Allow roughly 45–50 minutes for this question. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark allocation and the balance between AOs.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the closed-book exam, memorise 10–12 short quotations that cover the play’s key themes and characters. The best quotations are short (under 10 words), versatile (usable for multiple themes), and contain interesting language to analyse. For example, “It’s the only way to forget” works for essays on Stanhope, on fear, on coping, or on the psychological effects of war. Always analyse individual word choices: why “forget” rather than “cope”? Why “the only way” rather than “a good way”?
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play’s themes — heroism, fear, class, friendship, and futility — are interconnected. The best essays explore these connections rather than treating them in isolation.
  • Sherriff redefines heroism as endurance rather than glory, and presents fear as universal — the only difference between characters is how they cope.
  • For the Section B essay: use the given quotation as a springboard, range across the whole play, embed context into every paragraph, and spend 45–50 minutes. Memorise 10–12 short, versatile quotations.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Sherriff presents the theme of futility through the structure and ending of the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): The raid costs Osborne’s life but achieves nothing that prevents the attack. Raleigh dies. The dugout is destroyed. The play offers no resolution or meaning. Structurally, it ends where it began — with shells and darkness. This circular quality mirrors the futility of the Western Front. The absence of catharsis is a deliberate artistic choice.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with examples.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Sherriff use the public-school background of the officers to explore themes of class and leadership?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Stanhope, Raleigh, and Osborne share a public-school background that taught them duty, composure, and the stiff upper lip. These values sustain them but also suppress their emotions. Trotter’s lower-middle-class background and eventual promotion suggest the class system is fracturing. The Colonel’s detachment represents the upper hierarchy’s indifference to the men below.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear points with some context.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Basic comments.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Which quotation from the play would be most useful for an essay about the theme of fear? Explain your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): “You think there’s no limit to what a man can bear?” is the strongest choice. The rhetorical question reveals Stanhope’s desperation. “Limit” implies he is near breaking point. “A man” universalises the experience beyond Stanhope. It connects to shell shock, the officer class’s code, and the play’s argument that fear is universal.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of a relevant quotation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the play’s themes are better understood as interconnected rather than separate. Give an example of two themes that overlap.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Heroism and futility overlap: the men’s courage (Osborne leading the raid, Stanhope carrying on) is admirable but ultimately pointless — Osborne dies and the attack comes anyway. Friendship and loss are inseparable: Stanhope’s love for Osborne makes his death devastating. Treating themes as interconnected produces more nuanced arguments.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of two themes without showing how they connect.

glossary_terms.definition: Brave or noble conduct, traditionally associated with military valour but questioned and complicated throughout the play.
A sense of moral obligation to serve one’s country and fulfil one’s responsibilities, especially in wartime.
An overwhelming feeling of distress or terror, often caused by an awareness of danger.
A mental health condition triggered by traumatic events, characterised by flashbacks, anxiety, and emotional withdrawal. Known as shell shock during WWI.
Fee-paying secondary schools in England, historically associated with the upper and upper-middle classes, which trained boys for leadership roles.
A bond of loyalty and mutual support between people who share a common experience, especially among soldiers.
The quality of being pointless or producing no useful result, a key theme in WWI literature that questions whether the war’s enormous human cost achieved anything meaningful.
The rigid ranking system of the military, where orders flow from senior officers to junior officers and then to soldiers.
